title: The last judgment (CCC 1038–1041)
hook: all will be made plain, and God's justice and mercy seen

segments.voice: Yesterday, the particular judgment: each person, at death, meeting Christ. Your line was face to face. What did your day look like, seen in full? Day one thousand eighty-four.

"Lord, when did we see thee hungry?" That's the question at the center of a story Jesus tells near the end of Matthew's Gospel, just before the account of his Passion begins. A king sits on his throne with all the nations gathered in front of him, and he separates them, the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Then he explains why. And here's the strange part: both groups ask the same question. The ones he praises are surprised. The ones he sends away are surprised too. Nobody saw it coming. Yesterday was one person meeting Christ alone. Today is the whole human story, all at once, out in the open.
screen: `WHEN DID WE SEE THEE HUNGRY?` → `SHEEP AND GOATS.` → `EVERYONE IS SURPRISED.`

segments.voice: Here's the king's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Christ was there all along, in the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the prisoner. The people who fed them didn't know it. That's the first thing the Catechism draws from this scene: the last judgment shows what was really going on the whole time. Second, it's public. The Catechism teaches that at the end of time, after the resurrection of the dead, every person will stand before Christ, and the truth of each life, and its relationship with God, will be laid bare. Jesus says it in Luke: "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed: nor hid, that shall not be known." Third, it's about the whole story, not just one life. The Catechism says that on that day people will see the meaning of all of history, and how God's providence led everything toward its end. And it says something hopeful about why: the last judgment will show that God's justice wins over every injustice his creatures have done, and that his love is stronger than death. Every wrong that was hidden, every victim nobody listened to, finally seen. Fourth, what it asks for now. The Catechism reads this teaching as a call to turn toward God while there is time, and quotes Saint Paul: "Behold, now is the acceptable time." The scene isn't given to frighten people about the end. In the Catholic reading, it's given so that people live today as if everything will one day be seen. In Catholic belief, it will.
screen: `YOU DID IT TO ME.` · `NOTHING COVERED THAT SHALL NOT BE REVEALED.` · `JUSTICE AND LOVE, SEEN.` · `NOW IS THE ACCEPTABLE TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live transparently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one part of your life you keep a little hidden, not because it's private, but because you'd rather nobody looked closely. A habit, a way you talk about someone, a small shortcut. Ask one plain question: if this were made plain tomorrow, would I change it? If the answer is yes, choose one small step toward changing it. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to live in the open. If you don't, just let the question sit with you. The bell holds the time.
The last judgment. Catholics believe that at the end of time, Christ will judge all people, and everything hidden will be made plain, showing God's justice and his mercy. Today's word.
Your line: all made plain. Today, do one kind thing for someone who can't pay you back, the way the people in the story fed the hungry without knowing who it was. Day one thousand eighty-four.

screen: `DAY 1084 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A NEW HEAVEN AND EARTH.`

howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed at Mass that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and Matthew's scene of the sheep and the goats is among the Gospels read at Mass.

notes: CCC paraphrased (1038 resurrection then judgment, Matthew 25; 1039 the truth of each relationship with God laid bare; 1040 meaning of history, providence, justice over injustice, love stronger than death, only the Father knows the day; 1041 call to conversion, 2 Corinthians 6:2). Confirm.
Hook places the story 'a few days before his death', following Matthew 26:1–2 (after these words, the Pasch in two days). Confirm.
Confirm Challoner wording of Matthew 25:37 and 25:40, Luke 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 6:2. In 25:37 the full verse reads 'Lord, when did we see thee hungry, and fed thee'.
howItsDone: Matthew 25:31–46 is the Gospel for the Solemnity of Christ the King in Year A of the Sunday lectionary; the script says only 'near the end of the liturgical year'. Confirm.
